questions.question: If a network round trip normally takes about 1 ms, what does an asynchronous packet network guarantee about the maximum delay?

options.text: Nothing at all — the delay is unbounded
That it stays within roughly ten times the normal case
That it is bounded by the TCP retransmission timeout
That it is bounded by the size of the switch's buffer

questions.explanation: Asynchronous networks have unbounded delays: implementations try to deliver packets as quickly as possible, but there is no upper limit on the time it may take, which is why no timeout can distinguish a dead node from a slow one.

questions.question: Which of these topics are about things going wrong in a data system, rather than about data formats changing over time? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Replica failover when a leader node becomes unavailable
Replication lag causing reads to return stale data
Concurrency control to stop transactions racing each other
Schema evolution keeping old and new encodings compatible

questions.explanation: As we come to understand various edge cases that can occur in real systems, we get better at handling them.

optionExplanations.a: Leader unavailability forces a replicated system to detect failure, choose a replacement and redirect traffic without creating two active leaders.
optionExplanations.b: Asynchronous propagation lets followers return older values, so applications need explicit guarantees such as read-after-write or monotonic reads.
optionExplanations.c: Concurrent transactions can invalidate one another's assumptions, requiring isolation mechanisms that prevent or detect harmful interleavings.
optionExplanations.d: Schema evolution concerns compatibility between old and new data encodings; it is a change-management topic rather than one of these runtime fault cases.

questions.question: Algorithm correctness is often split into safety and liveness properties. How must each of them hold?

options.text: Safety must always hold; liveness may be qualified, such as 'eventually'
Liveness must always hold; safety is only required to hold eventually
Both must hold at every moment, with no caveats permitted at all
Safety governs performance, while liveness governs data integrity

questions.explanation: Safety is roughly 'nothing bad happens': once it is violated you can point at the exact moment it broke, and the damage cannot be undone. Liveness is 'something good eventually happens', and such properties are usually allowed caveats — for example, a response is required only if a majority of nodes have not crashed.

questions.question: What is the main difference between distributed systems and software on a single computer?

options.text: That there are lots of new and exciting ways for things to go wrong
That performance becomes considerably harder to predict
That the codebase grows larger and harder to test properly
That all data must be serialized before it can be sent

questions.explanation: A single machine presents relatively stable abstractions for memory, time, and execution. Distribution adds independent failures, unreliable communication, and incomplete knowledge, so combinations of otherwise ordinary events create new failure modes.

questions.question: When faults are inevitable, how is the engineer's task best defined?

options.text: To build systems that do their job despite everything going wrong
To eliminate every possible fault from the system design
To detect faults as quickly as they can possibly be detected
To document every failure mode before the system is built

questions.explanation: Fault tolerance does not make components infallible. It means the system continues to meet specified guarantees despite the faults included in its design assumptions.

questions.question: Which three problem areas make up the core uncertainty of a distributed system?

options.text: Unreliable networks, unreliable clocks, and knowledge, truth and lies
Replication, partitioning and distributed transactions
Consensus, total ordering and atomic commit protocols
Batch processing, stream processing and the future of data systems

questions.explanation: Network loss, clock uncertainty and process pauses make remote observations ambiguous. Studying these pessimistic cases is necessary because reliable algorithms must remain correct even when ordinary intuitions about time and liveness fail.

questions.question: How does a program running on a single computer behave when something goes wrong?

options.text: Predictably: either it works or it doesn't, rarely something in between
Unpredictably, because of variability in the underlying hardware
Predictably, but only while the machine is under light load
It always fails partially, exactly as a distributed system does

questions.explanation: There is no fundamental reason why software on a single computer should be flaky: when the hardware is working correctly, the same operation always produces the same result — it is deterministic.

questions.question: When a single computer does have a hardware problem, what is the usual consequence?

options.text: Total failure — a kernel panic, a blue screen, or a failure to boot
Partial degradation, in which wrong results are returned to callers
Silent data corruption that produces no visible symptom at all
Reduced throughput, while operation remains entirely correct

questions.explanation: Examples given include a kernel panic, a blue screen of death, failure to start up, and memory corruption from a loose connector.

questions.question: Why is the all-or-nothing behaviour of a computer described as deliberate?

options.text: Because a wrong result is harder to handle than an outright crash
Because crashing is cheaper to implement than error recovery
Because operating systems cannot detect partial faults
The behaviour is not deliberate at all; it is an accident of hardware design

questions.explanation: Escalating partial failure into total failure is a design choice made to keep results trustworthy.

questions.question: What do deterministic computer abstractions hide?

options.text: Messy and unpredictable physical behavior
They hide network latency, and the goal dates from the 1970s
They hide concurrency, and the goal dates from the 1990s
They hide nothing at all; the physical reality is fully exposed

questions.explanation: Hardware and operating systems normally mask bit errors, timing variation, and partial execution so software can reason about clean abstractions. Across machines, network loss and independent pauses make that illusion impossible to preserve completely.

questions.question: The Coda Hale anecdote lists failures from one operator's 'limited experience'. Which does it include? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Network partitions in a single datacenter, PDU failures and switch failures
Accidental power cycles of whole racks, whole-datacenter backbone failures and whole-datacenter power failures
A hypoglycemic driver smashing his Ford pickup truck into a datacenter's HVAC system
A software bug in the database engine that quietly returns wrong results to every caller

questions.explanation: And he adds 'I'm not even an ops guy' — in the physical world, a remarkably wide range of things can go wrong.

optionExplanations.a: Ordinary datacenter infrastructure can fail at several layers, including network partitions, power-distribution units and switches, even without a regional disaster.
optionExplanations.b: Human mistakes and shared backbone or power dependencies can affect an entire rack or datacenter, demonstrating correlated rather than independent faults.
optionExplanations.c: The vehicle striking HVAC equipment is an intentionally memorable example of an external physical event disrupting critical datacenter infrastructure.
optionExplanations.d: Quietly returning wrong results is a Byzantine-style software failure, but it is not one of the concrete physical and operational incidents in the anecdote.

questions.question: Define partial failure, and say what makes it difficult.

options.text: Partial failure: some parts broken while others work, unpredictably
Partial failure means half the nodes are down; the difficulty is capacity
Partial failure means data is partially written; the difficulty is corruption
Partial failure means slow responses; the difficulty is latency

questions.explanation: This nondeterminism and possibility of partial failures is what makes distributed systems hard to work with.

questions.question: Which statements correctly characterize high-performance computing and cloud computing? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: High-performance computing: supercomputers with thousands of CPUs, typically used for computationally intensive scientific computing tasks such as weather forecasting or molecular dynamics
Cloud computing: often associated with multi-tenant datacenters, commodity computers connected with an IP network (often Ethernet), elastic/on-demand resource allocation, and metered billing
Traditional enterprise datacenters lie somewhere between these extremes
Cloud computing is a precisely defined technical term with a single agreed industry meaning behind it

questions.explanation: Cloud computing is a broad family rather than one precise architecture. It is commonly associated with commodity machines, elastic provisioning, multi-tenancy and conventional packet-network communication.

optionExplanations.a: High-performance computing uses tightly coupled supercomputers to run intensive scientific workloads whose communication and checkpointing patterns are often predictable.
optionExplanations.b: Multi-tenancy, commodity nodes, Ethernet/IP networking, elastic allocation and metered billing are common cloud characteristics rather than a strict formal definition.
optionExplanations.c: Enterprise datacenters often mix specialized ownership and operations with commodity networked servers, placing them between the two stylized extremes.
optionExplanations.d: Cloud computing has no single precise technical definition; treating the associated characteristics as a mandatory industry specification is the misconception.

questions.question: How does a supercomputer handle a fault?

options.text: Checkpoint to durable storage and restart the whole job on failure
It routes around the failed node automatically with no interruption
It replicates all state, so no checkpoint is needed
It ignores the failure and continues with degraded results

questions.explanation: A tightly coupled HPC job can treat one component failure as failure of the whole computation: restore a durable checkpoint, repair or replace hardware, and restart. An online service usually cannot stop every user request while one node is repaired.

questions.question: How do internet services differ from supercomputer batch jobs during faults?

options.text: Services must stay responsive; batch jobs can stop and resume
Each is an online service that cannot tolerate any period of downtime
Each is an offline batch job that may be restarted freely on failure
Internet services are offline batch jobs; supercomputers are online

questions.explanation: Availability requirements are what rule out stop-and-repair for internet services.

questions.question: What hardware model distinguishes cloud systems from supercomputers?

options.text: Clouds use commodity nodes and conventional packet networks
Each is built from commodity hardware and communicates by message passing
Each is built from specialized hardware and communicates by shared memory
Supercomputers use commodity hardware while cloud services use specialized

questions.explanation: Reliable specialized nodes with shared memory versus unreliable commodity nodes with messages.

questions.question: Why do supercomputers use specialized network topologies?

options.text: They optimize known, predictable communication patterns
Each uses Clos topologies, chosen for their high bisection bandwidth
Each uses meshes and toruses suited to known communication patterns
Datacenters use toruses while supercomputers are built on Ethernet

questions.explanation: High-performance computing workloads often have predictable communication patterns, so a purpose-built mesh or torus can optimize those exchanges. Datacenters need flexible Clos networks for varied traffic.

questions.question: Why does whole-system restart become impractical at large scale?

options.text: Some component is likely to be broken almost continuously
Scale reduces the probability of brokenness, because of redundancy
Scale has no effect on the probability that something is broken
Scale makes the give-up-and-restart approach cheaper than repair

questions.explanation: Even rare per-node faults become routine somewhere in a large fleet. Restarting every healthy node whenever one component fails would destroy availability and waste nearly completed work.

questions.question: What operational benefits follow from tolerating failed nodes? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Rolling upgrade: restarting one node at a time, while the service continues serving users without interruption
In a cloud environment, if one virtual machine is not performing well, you can just kill it and request a new one, hoping that the new one will be faster
Faults become impossible once the job has been checkpointed to durable storage
Checkpointing becomes unnecessary, since the computed state can never be lost

questions.explanation: Cloud services tolerate losing commodity nodes and replace them while the service continues. Supercomputer jobs may instead checkpoint state, stop after a fault, repair resources and resume.

optionExplanations.a: If other nodes continue serving, operators can restart and upgrade one node at a time without turning a software rollout into a user-visible outage.
optionExplanations.b: Treating virtual machines as replaceable lets operators discard a degraded instance and provision another while replicas preserve the service.
optionExplanations.c: A checkpoint preserves recoverable computation state but cannot prevent hardware, network or software faults from occurring afterward.
optionExplanations.d: Tolerating node failure does not make computed state indestructible; checkpointing or durable replication may still be needed for recovery.

questions.question: Why does geographic distribution make things worse?

options.text: Because communication most likely goes over the internet
Because clocks cannot be synchronized across distance
Because data cannot be replicated across regions
It does not make things worse

questions.explanation: Geo-distributed systems communicate across networks operated by many independent parties. Compared with one controlled datacenter, routes, latency and failures are less observable and predictable.

questions.question: What failure model must practical distributed software accept?

options.text: Partial failure, with only some components faulty
We must eliminate partial failure through better hardware
We must accept that distributed systems cannot be reliable
We must use supercomputer-style checkpointing

questions.explanation: Redundancy, retry, and isolation can create a reliable service from unreliable parts only within a defined fault model. No design can promise survival after every replica, network path, and backup fails together.

questions.question: Why must even a small system think about partial failure? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because it is important to consider a wide range of possible faults — even fairly unlikely ones — and to artificially create such situations in your testing environment to see what happens; in distributed systems, suspicion, pessimism, and paranoia pay off

Because in a distributed system, even if most of the components are working correctly most of the time, sooner or later some part of the system will become faulty, so fault handling must be part of the software design
Because you, as operator of the software, need to know what behavior to expect from the software in the case of a fault
Because it is wise to assume faults are rare and simply hope for the best whenever one does occur in production

questions.explanation: Partial failure is unavoidable, so software should define how it behaves when some components fail. Treating every fault as catastrophic merely because a perfectly fault-free system is impossible is unwise.

optionExplanations.a: Fault injection exposes recovery behavior before production and tests unlikely but plausible cases that normal happy-path testing rarely reaches.
optionExplanations.b: Even a few components eventually experience crashes, pauses or network loss, so partial-failure behavior is part of normal long-running system design.
optionExplanations.c: Operators need a predictable, documented response to faults so they can distinguish safe degradation from corruption or a stuck cluster.
optionExplanations.d: Rarity is not protection over a system's lifetime; hoping for the best leaves untested recovery paths to fail unpredictably when the fault eventually occurs.

questions.question: The 'Building a Reliable System from Unreliable Components' box names an intuition and rejects it. Which?

options.text: That a system is only as reliable as its least reliable component
That adding redundancy always improves overall reliability
That reliability is directly proportional to money spent
That software can never be more reliable than its hardware

questions.explanation: A system can be more reliable than any individual component by adding redundancy and recovery. Reliability depends on failure independence and design, not simply on the least reliable part.

questions.question: How do error-correcting codes and TCP mask unreliable lower layers, and which limits remain? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Error-correcting codes allow digital data to be transmitted accurately across a communication channel that occasionally gets some bits wrong, for example due to radio interference on a wireless network

IP is unreliable — it may drop, delay, duplicate, or reorder packets — but TCP provides a more reliable transport layer on top: missing packets are retransmitted, duplicates are eliminated, and packets are reassembled into the order in which they were sent

Error correction can handle a small number of single-bit errors, but if your signal is swamped by interference there is a fundamental limit to how much data you can get through your communication channel
TCP can hide packet loss and reordering, and its retransmission mechanism removes variable network delay along with them

questions.explanation: TCP cannot remove delay — it can hide packet loss, duplication and reordering, but not the time the network takes. Note which of IP's four sins TCP does not fix: delay. That omission is the seed of the entire unreliable-networks discussion.

optionExplanations.a: Error-correcting codes add redundancy that lets a receiver reconstruct data after a limited number of bit errors, masking a noisy physical channel.
optionExplanations.b: TCP retransmits missing data, removes duplicates and restores byte order, presenting applications with a more reliable stream than raw IP packets.
optionExplanations.c: Redundancy has a finite correction capacity; sufficiently severe interference exceeds the channel's information limit and cannot be repaired.
optionExplanations.d: Retransmission can make delivery take longer and network queues remain variable, so TCP improves reliability without creating a latency bound.

questions.question: If the higher-level system is not perfect, why bother with a leaky abstraction?

options.text: Because it makes the remaining faults easier to reason about
Because a leaky abstraction is always better than none
Because the abstraction can be made perfect with enough effort
You shouldn't bother; leaky abstractions should be removed

questions.explanation: Reliable components and controlled networks reduce how often difficult faults occur and narrow the cases software must handle. They cannot eliminate partial failure or ambiguous remote observations entirely.

questions.question: What kind of systems does Part II focus on, and what does the architecture forbid?

options.text: Shared-nothing: machines with private memory, communicating only by network
Shared-disk systems, in which every machine reaches one storage array
Shared-memory systems, communicating by remote direct memory access
Single-machine systems, in which there is no network at all

questions.explanation: Shared-nothing became dominant for internet services because it is comparatively cheap, requiring no special hardware; it can make use of commoditized cloud computing services; and it can achieve high reliability through redundancy across multiple geographically distributed datacenters.

questions.question: Define an asynchronous packet network.

options.text: Asynchronous packet networks, with no guarantee of arrival or timing
A network with bounded delay and guaranteed message delivery
A network in which messages are always delivered in order
A circuit-switched network with bandwidth reserved per connection

questions.explanation: Asynchronous packet networks neither promise delivery nor bound delay. A sender therefore cannot distinguish a lost message from one delayed for an unexpectedly long time.

questions.question: You send a request and expect a response. Which failures are possible? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Your request may have been lost, perhaps someone unplugged a network cable; or it may be waiting in a queue and will be delivered later, perhaps the network or the recipient is overloaded

The remote node may have failed, perhaps it crashed or was powered down; or it may have temporarily stopped responding, perhaps because of a long garbage collection pause, but will start responding again later
The remote node may have processed the request and returned a response which arrives corrupted and is then silently accepted as valid
The remote node may have processed the request, but its response may be lost or delayed, perhaps by a switch fault, network overload, or overload on your own machine

questions.explanation: Silence cannot distinguish six cases: request lost or delayed, remote node failed or paused, and response lost or delayed. A timeout reveals uncertainty, not which stage failed or whether the operation took effect.

optionExplanations.a: A request can disappear before arrival or remain queued behind congestion, and both produce the same lack of response at the sender.
optionExplanations.b: A crashed node and a long-paused but healthy process are observationally identical until communication resumes or another source provides evidence.
optionExplanations.c: Corruption is a possible network concern, but transport and application checks usually detect it; it is not one of the six silence-producing stages described here.
optionExplanations.d: The server may complete the operation while its reply is lost or delayed, creating the dangerous ambiguous outcome in which retrying can duplicate effects.

questions.question: Why is a missing network response ambiguous?

options.text: Loss, delay and remote pauses produce the same silence
Because the network protocol has no support for acknowledgments
Because the sender's clock may be wrong about the send time
It can tell — TCP acknowledgments already provide exactly this

questions.explanation: No response is compatible with a lost or delayed request, a failed or paused receiver, and a lost or delayed response. The sender therefore cannot infer either node health or whether the operation took effect.

questions.question: What does a timeout tell you, and what residual uncertainty remains?

options.text: You give up waiting, still not knowing whether the request arrived
It tells you definitively that the remote node has died
It tells you the request was definitely not processed
It tells you the response was lost rather than the request

questions.explanation: When a timeout expires, the caller chooses to stop waiting; it has not learned what happened remotely. The request or response may still be delayed, and the operation may already have completed.

questions.question: What did the study of a medium-sized datacenter find?

options.text: About 12 faults per month, half per-machine and half per-rack
About 2 network faults per year, all of them at rack level
About 100 faults per month, all of them single-machine
Effectively none, which is why the study was published

questions.explanation: 12 per month is roughly 144 per year, split 72/72 between single-machine and rack-level.

questions.question: Does redundant networking gear help as much as you might hope?

options.text: No — redundancy reduced faults less than expected
Yes, redundancy eliminates network faults entirely
Yes, redundancy reduces faults proportionally to the number of paths
The study found redundancy increases faults

questions.explanation: Redundant network paths help with cable and equipment faults, but an operator can misconfigure all paths or disconnect the wrong component. Shared dependencies create correlated failures.

questions.question: How do public cloud networks compare with well-managed private datacenter networks?

options.text: EC2 is notorious for transient glitches; private datacenters can be stable
Private datacenter networks experience no network faults at all
EC2 turns out to be more reliable than a private datacenter
The two are equally unreliable, with no measurable difference

questions.explanation: Local datacenter networks are usually faster and more reliable than wide-area links, but they still lose, delay and reorder packets. The uncertainty is smaller in degree, not absent in kind.

questions.question: Which surprising network interface fault is worth knowing about?

options.text: An interface that dropped all inbound packets but sent outbound ones fine
An interface that silently duplicated every packet it sent
An interface that reordered packets but never dropped one
An interface that corrupted inbound packets but not outbound

questions.explanation: Connectivity can be asymmetric: A may reach B while B cannot reach A, or both may reach a third node. Such partial views make failure detection treacherous because no observer sees the complete network state.

questions.question: Which term avoids confusing a netsplit with data partitioning?

options.text: Network fault
It prefers 'netsplit' to avoid confusion with CAP
It prefers 'network partition' as the standard term
It uses all three terms interchangeably

questions.explanation: A disconnected region is often called a network partition or netsplit, but 'network fault' is broader and avoids collision with data partitioning, where a database is intentionally divided into shards.

questions.question: What happens when software meets an untested network fault? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The cluster could become deadlocked and permanently unable to serve requests, even when the network recovers
It could delete all of your data
It could silently corrupt only the most recent writes
It could duplicate every write exactly once on recovery

questions.explanation: If software is put in an unanticipated situation it may do arbitrary unexpected things. The second example is cited from an analysis of Redis Sentinel properties and failure scenarios.

optionExplanations.a: An untested state transition can leave nodes waiting on one another even after connectivity returns, turning a temporary fault into permanent service deadlock.
optionExplanations.b: A poorly designed failover or split-brain recovery path can accept destructive decisions, and real analyses have found scenarios capable of deleting data.
optionExplanations.c: Arbitrary bugs may corrupt data, but the narrowly specified outcome of corrupting only the most recent writes is not one of the supported examples.
optionExplanations.d: Recovery bugs can duplicate work, but guaranteeing exactly one duplicate of every write is an invented deterministic behavior rather than the cited failure mode.

questions.question: What distinguishes tolerating a network fault from merely handling it?

options.text: Tolerance continues useful service during the fault
They are the same thing under two different names
Tolerating means showing an error; handling means full recovery
Handling is unnecessary when the network is normally reliable enough

questions.explanation: Every system must define and test a recoverable response to network faults, even if that response is an error. Fault tolerance is the stronger property of continuing useful service while the fault persists.

questions.question: Why is automatic detection of faulty nodes needed? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A load balancer needs to stop sending requests to a node that is dead — take it out of rotation
In a distributed database with single-leader replication, if the leader fails, one of the followers needs to be promoted to be the new leader
To recompute the entire replication log from scratch after a failover
To synchronize the clocks across every node in the whole cluster

questions.explanation: Failure detectors and leader election both decide whether a silent node should still be trusted. An unreliable network cannot reveal whether that node is dead, partitioned, delayed or paused.

optionExplanations.a: A load balancer must remove an unavailable endpoint or it will continue sending user requests into repeated timeouts and failures.
optionExplanations.b: Single-leader availability depends on noticing leader loss and promoting a follower so the system regains a write authority.
optionExplanations.c: Failover normally continues from replicated state and log positions; recomputing the entire replication log is neither the purpose of failure detection nor required.
optionExplanations.d: Clock synchronization estimates time offsets and is a separate protocol; determining node liveness does not synchronize every machine's clock.

questions.question: What can a TCP RST or FIN establish after a failed request?

options.text: Connection state, not whether the application processed the request
You receive an ICMP echo reply confirming it was processed
You receive nothing at all, so a timeout is your only signal
You receive a full transaction log of what was processed

questions.explanation: RST or FIN can quickly reveal that the endpoint is not accepting the connection. It cannot prove whether a previous request took effect before the process failed, so application-level retries still need idempotence or deduplication.

questions.question: You can query switch management interfaces to detect link failures. When is that option ruled out? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If you're connecting via the internet
If you're in a shared datacenter with no access to the switches themselves
If you can't reach the management interface due to a network problem
If the remote machine is powered down, since a powered-down machine cannot be distinguished from a healthy one

questions.explanation: Switch telemetry is useful only when you control and can reach the relevant management plane. Internet paths, shared facilities, or a fault blocking that interface remove the signal. Even available link data cannot establish how far an application request progressed.

optionExplanations.a: An application using the public internet cannot query and correlate management data from every independently operated switch along the route.
optionExplanations.b: A tenant in a shared facility normally lacks administrative access to provider switches, so link telemetry cannot be its failure oracle.
optionExplanations.c: The same network fault being diagnosed may block access to the management interface, removing the supposedly independent source of evidence.
optionExplanations.d: A powered-down host may cause a switch port status change that management can report; it does not itself prevent querying the switch interface.

questions.question: What may a router send for a known-unreachable destination?

options.text: ICMP Destination Unreachable
An ICMP echo request, which is fully reliable
A TCP RST, which is definitive
Silence, since a router has no mechanism for reporting unreachability

questions.explanation: An ICMP unreachable message reflects one router's current knowledge and may itself be lost or delayed. It says nothing definitive about whether a remote application processed an earlier request.

questions.question: What counts as knowing that a request actually succeeded?

options.text: A positive response from the application itself
A TCP acknowledgment from the remote host is sufficient
The absence of an error response is sufficient evidence
A timeout that has not yet expired is sufficient evidence

questions.explanation: Rapid feedback about a remote node being down is useful but you can't count on it. The general procedure: you may get an error response at some level of the stack, but in general you have to assume that you will get no response at all — you can retry a few times, wait for a timeout to elapse, and eventually declare the node dead.

questions.question: What trade-off determines a network timeout?

options.text: Fast detection versus fewer false suspicions
Always use 30 seconds, the standard value
Always use the shortest possible timeout
Always use the longest tolerable timeout

questions.explanation: A short timeout enables quick failover but mistakes ordinary delay for failure more often. A long timeout reduces false suspicion but leaves real failures undetected longer.

questions.question: Why is prematurely declaring a node dead problematic?

options.text: Because the node may be alive and midway through an action
Because the node's data will be deleted when it is declared dead
Because the node will not be able to rejoin the cluster afterwards
Because the clocks on the two nodes will drift further apart

questions.explanation: Retrying an ambiguous request can repeat a non-idempotent side effect, such as charging a card twice, because the first attempt may have succeeded despite the lost response. Idempotency keys or deduplication are needed.

questions.question: Explain the cascading failure mechanism from premature timeouts.

options.text: Extra load on the remaining nodes, which can cascade into more failures
Premature timeouts reduce load, by shedding work early
Premature timeouts affect only the node that timed out
Cascading failure comes from long timeouts, not short ones

questions.explanation: If overload makes a healthy node slow, a timeout may redirect traffic to other nodes. The extra load slows those nodes too, creating a positive feedback loop and cascading outage.

questions.question: With one-way delay d and handling time r, what response-time bound follows?

options.text: 2d + r; for d = 20 ms and r = 100 ms, 140 ms
A total of d + r, which works out to 120 ms
A total of 2(d + r), which works out to 240 ms
A total of d + 2r, which works out to 220 ms

questions.explanation: The request consumes at most d, processing at most r, and the response another d. Under those fictional hard bounds, silence after 140 ms proves that the request path, response path, or node violated the model.

questions.question: Why is 2d + r not a safe hard timeout in ordinary distributed systems?

options.text: Neither network delay nor process time has a hard upper bound
Only the network assumption fails; response times are bounded
Only the response-time assumption fails; networks are bounded
Both assumptions hold in practice, which is why 2d + r is the standard timeout

questions.explanation: Networks and processes are usually fast, but neither packet delay nor process pause has a guaranteed maximum. A probabilistic observation cannot justify the hard 2d + r bound.

questions.question: What is the dominant cause of packet-delay variability?

options.text: Variable queueing throughout the network path
The analogy is air traffic control; the cause is routing changes
The analogy is postal delivery; the cause is packet loss
The analogy is water pipes; the cause is bandwidth limits

questions.explanation: Propagation distance and link bandwidth are comparatively stable. Variable queues at switches, operating systems, hypervisors and receivers dominate the unpredictable tail of packet latency.

questions.question: Where does queueing arise in a packet network? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At switches whose outgoing links receive simultaneous traffic
At a destination whose CPU is not ready for the application
At a hypervisor while the destination virtual machine is paused
At the sender: TCP flow control removes queueing altogether by refusing to transmit anything until the network path is completely idle

questions.explanation: Flow control (also called congestion avoidance or backpressure) limits a node's own send rate rather than waiting for an idle network — and it moves the queueing into the sender. Four sources, at the switch, the destination CPU, the hypervisor and the sender.

optionExplanations.a: When several inputs target one outgoing link, the switch serializes those packets in a buffer and may drop them if that queue fills.
optionExplanations.b: After arrival, packets wait in operating-system buffers when all CPU cores are busy and the application cannot consume them yet.
optionExplanations.c: A paused virtual machine cannot drain incoming data, so the hypervisor or virtual network layer buffers it until that VM is scheduled.
optionExplanations.d: TCP flow control throttles sending and can create a sender-side queue; it does not wait for a completely idle path or eliminate queueing.

questions.question: What delay does TCP loss recovery add for an application?

options.text: The retransmission timeout before TCP resends
TCP never retransmits, so the application must handle the loss
The application sees the loss itself, though not the delay
TCP retransmits immediately, without waiting for any timeout

questions.explanation: The application first waits through the original network delay, then TCP waits for its adaptive loss-detection timeout before retransmitting. Reliable delivery therefore adds delay when packets are lost.

questions.question: Why can real-time audio prefer UDP to TCP?

options.text: Late audio may be less useful than missing audio
UDP eliminates all delay variability
UDP performs flow control but not retransmission
UDP is more reliable than TCP

questions.explanation: Dropping reliability reduces some sources of delay but not queueing or scheduling.

questions.question: Why is retransmission pointless in a VoIP call?

options.text: Because retransmitting data that is already too late is pointless
Because UDP forbids retransmission at the protocol level
Because audio packets are too large to be retransmitted
Because voice data is not sensitive to errors in the first place

questions.explanation: For live audio or video, data arriving after its playback deadline is useless. UDP avoids TCP's retransmission wait, though it cannot remove network queueing or scheduling pauses.

questions.question: Why does latency rise sharply near maximum utilization?

options.text: Little spare capacity remains to drain traffic bursts
Because switches drop more packets at low utilization
Because TCP disables flow control near capacity
Because CPU scheduling becomes deterministic near capacity

questions.explanation: Queue growth is nonlinear in utilization, which is why tail latency explodes near saturation.

questions.question: What is a noisy neighbor in a multi-tenant system?

options.text: Another tenant whose load creates unpredictable queueing
Only the network links are shared, and the effect is called congestion
Only the CPUs are shared, and the effect is called steal time
Tenants in a public cloud share nothing, which is what makes latency predictable

questions.explanation: Tenants share links, switches, interfaces, CPUs and storage while having little visibility into one another. A noisy neighbor can suddenly fill queues and produce unpredictable latency.

questions.question: What is the right procedure for choosing a timeout?

options.text: Measure round-trip times over time and derive the timeout from them
Use the maximum round-trip time observed on a single machine
Use whatever default value the database vendor recommends
Use the median of a one-minute sample of round-trip times

questions.explanation: Adaptive failure detection learns the observed latency distribution and increases suspicion as silence becomes unusual. This responds better to changing jitter than a guessed universal constant.

questions.question: What is preferable to one fixed failure-detection timeout?

options.text: Adaptive suspicion based on observed delay and jitter
A fixed exponential backoff, as used in HBase and Kafka clients
A fixed 30-second timeout, as used by ZooKeeper for its sessions
An unbounded wait, as used by Riak when routing a request

questions.explanation: Recent round-trip samples establish a changing delay distribution. A detector can raise suspicion gradually when silence becomes unusual instead of treating one fixed threshold as correct for every load and network condition.

questions.question: Which comparison case shows that networks could in principle be made reliable?

options.text: The traditional fixed-line telephone network
The postal system, which guarantees delivery
The electrical grid, which guarantees voltage
The air traffic control network

questions.explanation: A network that does deliver bounded latency, which invites the question of why datacenters can't.

questions.question: What bandwidth does the stated ISDN circuit calculation yield?

options.text: 64 kbit/s from 4,000 frames/s times 16 bits
8,000 frames per second with 8 bits each, giving 64,000 bits per second
4,000 frames per second with 8 bits each, giving 32,000 bits per second
1,000 frames per second with 64 bits each

questions.explanation: 4,000 frames per second is one frame every 250 microseconds; 4,000 times 16 bits is 64,000 bits per second.

questions.question: Why does a circuit give bounded delay?

options.text: Because reserved space per hop removes queueing entirely
Because circuit routers are faster than packet routers
Because the circuit uses UDP in place of TCP framing
Because the volume of audio data is small enough to fit

questions.explanation: A circuit reserves bandwidth along every hop before communication begins. Competing traffic cannot consume that allocation, so data need not wait for capacity on the reserved path.

questions.question: Contrast a telephone circuit with a TCP connection.

options.text: A circuit reserves bandwidth nobody else can use; TCP shares it opportunistically
Both reserve bandwidth; a TCP connection simply reserves less of it
Each is opportunistic, and the circuit merely receives scheduling priority
A TCP connection reserves its bandwidth even while sitting idle

questions.explanation: Circuit switching reserves a fixed slice of capacity for the call. Packet switching shares capacity opportunistically among active senders, improving utilization at the cost of queueing.

questions.question: Why can't Ethernet and IP promise a maximum round-trip time?

options.text: Because packet switching brings queueing and so unbounded delays
Because Ethernet is too slow to carry reserved circuits
Because the IP protocol is stateless between packets
They can do so, but implementations choose not to enable it

questions.explanation: Without an end-to-end reservation, packets compete for each link and may queue behind bursts. Since queue length and retransmission behavior lack a hard bound, latency lacks one too.

questions.question: What does InfiniBand link-layer flow control accomplish?

options.text: It reduces queueing but does not eliminate it
Only MPLS, since InfiniBand is purely a storage protocol
Only Token Ring, since InfiniBand implements circuit switching
Such hybrid protocols were proposed but never actually built or deployed

questions.explanation: InfiniBand can apply flow control before buffers overflow, limiting some loss and queue growth. Traffic still competes for finite links, so waiting is reduced rather than eliminated.

questions.question: How can circuits be emulated on packet networks?

options.text: Quality of service and admission control
By disabling TCP flow control
By reserving IP addresses per flow
Circuits cannot be emulated on packet networks

questions.explanation: Traffic engineering can make latency exceedances rare and quantify them statistically. A high percentile is still not the absolute worst-case bound required by a synchronous model.

questions.question: What trade-off follows from reserving one fixed slot per telephone call?

options.text: Predictable bandwidth but wasted idle capacity
All 10,000 slots are shared dynamically, giving no guarantee
The wire adapts its capacity to the number of calls
Unused slots are reallocated to active calls

questions.explanation: A reserved call slot provides predictable bandwidth even while the caller is silent. That unused capacity cannot serve someone else, so deterministic service trades away utilization.

questions.question: Why does the internet dynamically share bandwidth among packets?

options.text: To raise utilization and lower cost per byte
It reserves bandwidth per flow, with no queueing and no cost benefit
It allocates capacity round-robin, which bounds the delay
It does not allocate bandwidth between senders at all

questions.explanation: Dynamic sharing lets idle capacity serve active flows, raising utilization and lowering cost per byte. Bursts then compete in queues, so users accept variable delay for that efficiency.

questions.question: What latency trade-off comes from dynamic CPU scheduling?

options.text: Higher utilization with variable scheduling delays
CPUs are always statically partitioned, unlike networks
CPU scheduling has no effect on latency
The argument does not carry over to CPUs

questions.explanation: Operating systems share CPU cores among threads and virtual machines to keep hardware busy. Run queues and preemption improve utilization but make each task's scheduling delay variable.

questions.question: What resource policy makes hard latency guarantees easier?

options.text: Static resource partitioning
Variable delays are a law of nature and cannot be avoided
Static partitioning is always cheaper
Dynamic partitioning gives both low cost and bounded delay

questions.explanation: Static allocation can provide stronger latency guarantees, so variable delay is not physically inevitable. Dynamic sharing is normally chosen because its higher utilization is much cheaper.

questions.question: Where is quality of service currently not available to you?

options.text: In multi-tenant datacenters, public clouds, and over the internet
Only inside private datacenters that you own outright
Only on wireless networks, where interference dominates
Quality of service is enabled everywhere by default today

questions.explanation: IP forwarding dynamically shares links per packet, but network operators can buy dedicated capacity and establish longer-lived inter-network routes. Those arrangements resemble circuits at a network scale, not per host connection.

questions.question: True or false: an asynchronous network has bounded delay; a synchronous network avoids queueing because bandwidth is reserved at every hop; TCP turns an unbounded-delay network into a bounded-delay one; statistically bounded delay is the same as bounded delay.

options.text: False, true, false, false
True, true, true, true
False, false, true, true
True, false, false, true

questions.explanation: A synchronous model assumes known finite bounds on network delay, process pauses and clock error. It does not assume zero latency, perfect clocks or failure-free nodes.

questions.question: Which questions do applications use clocks to answer? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Has this request timed out yet? What's the 99th percentile response time of this service?
How many queries per second did this service handle on average in the last five minutes? How long did the user spend on our site?
When was this article published? At what date and time should the reminder email be sent? — both answered with a monotonic clock
When does this cache entry expire? What is the timestamp on this error message in the log file?

questions.explanation: Duration questions such as timeout measurement need a monotonic clock, while dates, logs and schedules need a time-of-day clock. The distinction is elapsed interval versus calendar point.

optionExplanations.a: Timeouts and response percentiles compare elapsed durations, so a monotonic clock avoids errors from wall-clock synchronization jumps.
optionExplanations.b: Rates over five minutes and time spent on a site are also elapsed-interval measurements rather than questions about a calendar timestamp.
optionExplanations.c: Publication and reminder times are real-world calendar points and therefore require a time-of-day clock; a machine-local monotonic value has no shared epoch.
optionExplanations.d: Cache expiry may be implemented with elapsed time, while a log timestamp needs calendar time; both are legitimate clock-dependent application questions.

questions.question: What is the core reason time is tricky in a distributed system?

options.text: Because a message takes time to cross the network
Because clocks are cheap and therefore inaccurate
Because time zones differ between machines
Because leap seconds are unpredictable

questions.explanation: A received timestamp combines the sender's clock error with unknown network delay. Even synchronized clocks therefore cannot reliably reveal the exact order of closely spaced distributed events.

questions.question: What hardware provides a computer's local clock signal?

options.text: A quartz crystal oscillator
An atomic clock, synchronized by GPS directly
A software counter, synchronized by the operating system
A network timestamp, with no local device

questions.explanation: Quartz oscillation turns physical vibration into clock ticks, but temperature and manufacturing variation cause drift. NTP compares several external time sources so a client can estimate error and reject disagreeing servers.

questions.question: Define the time-of-day clock precisely.

options.text: The current date and time by some calendar — wall-clock time
It returns nanoseconds since the computer was started
It returns a monotonically increasing counter with no calendar meaning
It returns seconds since the year 2000 including leap seconds

questions.explanation: A time-of-day clock is sometimes called a real-time clock because it tracks calendar time. That name is unrelated to hard real-time operating systems, which guarantee deadlines.

questions.question: Why can't time-of-day clocks measure elapsed time? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Backward jumps: if the local clock is too far ahead of the NTP server, it may be forcibly reset and appear to jump back to a previous point in time
Leap seconds: they often ignore leap seconds, which makes the timeline inconsistent
They have coarse-grained resolution — for example moving forward only in steps of 10 ms on older Windows systems
The two kinds of clock cannot be synchronized with one another at all

questions.explanation: The jumps and leap-second handling make them unsuitable for measuring elapsed time; the resolution problem is less of a problem on recent systems. Time-of-day clocks are usually synchronized with NTP, which means a timestamp from one machine ideally means the same as on another.

optionExplanations.a: NTP may step an inaccurate wall clock backward, making a later reading numerically smaller and producing a negative or understated elapsed duration.
optionExplanations.b: Leap-second omission or unusual handling makes the represented calendar timeline discontinuous, undermining simple subtraction as a duration measure.
optionExplanations.c: Coarse ticks quantize start and end readings, producing inaccurate short durations even when the wall clock does not jump.
optionExplanations.d: Operating systems maintain relationships between wall and monotonic clocks and can synchronize wall time externally; the problem is discontinuity, not total inability to correlate them.

questions.question: What property defines a monotonic clock?

options.text: It measures elapsed time without moving backward
It returns calendar time and is named for its monotone units
It is named for being monotonic in frequency, not in value
It always moves backward on resynchronization

questions.explanation: A monotonic clock never moves backward, making elapsed-time differences safe even during synchronization. A time-of-day clock may jump or slew to align with UTC and other machines.

questions.question: How do you use a monotonic clock value, and what is forbidden?

options.text: Read it twice and take the difference between the two values
You compare absolute values across machines to order events
You use the absolute value as a timestamp in stored data
You compare it against a time-of-day clock to detect drift

questions.explanation: Differences within a machine are meaningful; absolute values and cross-machine comparisons are not.

questions.question: What complication arises with multiple CPU sockets?

options.text: Separate timers per CPU socket, which the OS tries to hide
There is one timer shared by all sockets, so no complication arises
The operating system exposes each socket's timer separately
Multi-socket servers cannot provide a monotonic clock at all

questions.explanation: Operating systems hide imperfect hardware clocks through NTP corrections, slewing and separate clock APIs. Residual drift and synchronization uncertainty remain visible to distributed algorithms.

questions.question: How may NTP adjust a monotonic clock safely?

options.text: Slew its rate without making its value jump backward
Slewing means jumping the clock; NTP can slew but not adjust frequency
NTP can jump the monotonic clock but not slew it
NTP cannot affect the monotonic clock at all

questions.explanation: 0.05% is 500 parts per million, which over an hour is about 1.8 seconds and over a day about 43.2 seconds.

questions.question: Why are monotonic clocks fine in distributed systems?

options.text: Because measuring elapsed time needs no cross-node synchronization
Because monotonic clocks are synchronized by NTP across nodes
Because their absolute values are comparable between machines
Monotonic clocks are unsuitable here, and time-of-day clocks are preferred

questions.explanation: Monotonic clocks don't need synchronization, but time-of-day clocks need to be set according to an NTP server or other external time source in order to be useful.

questions.question: Which properties belong to the monotonic clock? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It is meaningless to compare its values across machines
It can be slewed but never jumped by NTP
It is the right tool for measuring a service's response time
It counts seconds since a calendar epoch

questions.explanation: Counting from a calendar epoch, jumping backward, needing an external time source, and being right for a 'when was this published' field all belong to the time-of-day clock.

optionExplanations.a: Each machine chooses its own monotonic origin, often boot-related, so raw values from different machines have no meaningful common reference.
optionExplanations.b: NTP may slightly change a monotonic clock's rate to correct drift, but preserving nondecreasing values keeps duration measurements safe.
optionExplanations.c: Response time is an elapsed interval on one machine, exactly the use case for a clock that cannot move backward.
optionExplanations.d: Seconds since a shared calendar epoch describe a time-of-day clock; monotonic clocks deliberately avoid claiming a real-world date.

questions.question: What error follows from a 200 ppm clock-drift assumption?

options.text: About 6 ms in 30 seconds, or 17 seconds in a day
Google assumes 2 ppm, giving 0.06 ms over 30 seconds
Google assumes 2000 ppm, giving 60 ms over 30 seconds
Clock drift is constant per machine regardless of temperature

questions.explanation: A 200 ppm rate error accumulates by 0.0002 seconds per second. Frequent synchronization limits the accumulated error, while a day without synchronization can create roughly 17 seconds of offset.

questions.question: What happens when a computer's clock differs too much from its NTP server?

options.text: It refuses to synchronize, or the local clock is forcibly reset
It slews the clock gradually, with no visible jump at all
It raises an error that is reported to every application
It shuts the machine down to prevent data corruption

questions.explanation: A node can also be accidentally firewalled off from NTP servers, and the misconfiguration may go unnoticed for some time — anecdotal evidence suggests this does happen in practice.

questions.question: What mainly limits NTP accuracy over the public internet?

options.text: Variable and asymmetric network delay
NTP is accurate to microseconds over the internet with no failure mode
NTP is accurate to 1 ms with spikes to 5 ms
NTP accuracy is independent of network delay

questions.explanation: The 35 ms minimum is about 350 times worse than the 100-microsecond MiFID II requirement, and the one-second spike is about 30 times worse again than the 35 ms floor.

questions.question: How can an NTP client tolerate a badly wrong time server?

options.text: Query several servers and discard majority-inconsistent outliers
NTP servers are never wrong; clients trust a single server
NTP servers can be off by milliseconds at most
Clients ignore all servers and use the local clock

questions.explanation: The NTP client contacts all configured servers, estimates their errors, and checks that a majority of servers agree on some time range — so a misconfigured server is detected as an outlier and excluded from synchronization.

questions.question: What happens to clocks in virtual machines?

options.text: The hardware clock is virtualized, so it can jump
Virtual machines have perfectly accurate clocks provided by the hypervisor
Virtual machine clocks run backward during pauses
Virtualization has no effect on clocks

questions.explanation: The same phenomenon as the hypervisor-induced network queueing, seen through the clock.

questions.question: How much can you trust the clock on a device you don't control?

options.text: Because you cannot trust the hardware clock on a device you don't control
Mobile clocks are synchronized by the carrier and always correct
Embedded devices are fitted with atomic clocks as standard
Users have no way of changing a device's hardware clock

questions.explanation: Clock synchronization is a security dependency as well as an accuracy dependency. An attacker who manipulates time can reorder logs, invalidate credentials or disrupt protocols even when hardware drift is small.

questions.question: What UTC accuracy does MiFID II require for high-frequency trading?

options.text: Within 100 microseconds
Within 100 milliseconds of UTC, to help with billing
Within 1 second of UTC, to help with audit logging
Within 1 microsecond of UTC, to help with order matching

questions.explanation: 100 microseconds is about 350 times tighter than the 35 ms minimum error seen when synchronizing over the internet, and about 70 times tighter than a few milliseconds on a local network.

questions.question: How can trading systems approach 100-microsecond UTC accuracy?

options.text: GPS, Precision Time Protocol and continuous offset monitoring
Through NTP alone, which does not fail when properly configured
Through an atomic clock in every machine, which cannot fail
It cannot be achieved at all with currently available hardware

questions.explanation: Specialized time sources and local precision protocols avoid much public-network uncertainty, but the guarantee depends on every layer being configured and monitored. A blocked time source lets ordinary quartz drift quickly exceed the target.

questions.question: True or false: a drifting clock usually announces itself by failing loudly; NTP can be more accurate than the network round-trip time; a misconfigured NTP server reporting a time off by hours will typically be ignored by clients; clock drift is a constant per machine.

options.text: False, false, true, false
True, true, true, true
False, true, false, true
True, false, true, false

questions.explanation: NTP clients improve robustness by querying several servers, estimating uncertainty intervals and rejecting outliers. They cannot assume every server is close to true time or trust the first response.

questions.question: Why are broken clocks worse than broken CPUs?

options.text: Because a bad clock breaks data subtly instead of stopping the node
A broken clock crashes the machine, whereas a broken CPU does not
A broken clock is always caught immediately by monitoring
The two kinds of fault are equally noticeable in practice

questions.explanation: A clock can drift far from UTC while its process continues serving requests normally. Because the failure is silent, systems need independent offset monitoring.

questions.question: If your software requires synchronized clocks, what is essential?

options.text: Monitor the clock offsets between all the machines
It is essential to use only monotonic clocks
It is essential to disable NTP
Monitoring is unnecessary once NTP has been correctly configured everywhere

questions.explanation: Once clock uncertainty exceeds the application's safe bound, timestamps can violate ordering assumptions. Quarantining that node is safer than continuing with misleading time.

questions.question: How can last-write-wins lose a causally later increment?

options.text: Clock skew gives the increment an earlier timestamp
It shows single-leader replication with a failover
It shows leaderless replication with quorum reads
It shows a partitioned database with cross-partition writes

questions.explanation: Separate leaders can accept causally related writes using different physical clocks. Last-write-wins then mistakes timestamp order for causal order and may discard the later operation.

questions.question: Can clocks within 3 ms still invert two causally ordered writes?

options.text: Yes; the later write can appear older
The skew is 300 ms and the timestamp error is 100 ms
The timestamps are correctly ordered, so there is no error
The skew is 3 seconds and the timestamp error is 1 second

questions.explanation: Events only 3 ms apart require clocks accurate to substantially better than 3 ms to preserve order. Even excellent millisecond-scale synchronization can invert causal writes.

questions.question: What does LWW do with x=1 at 42.004 and causally later x=2 at 42.003?

options.text: Keeps x=1 and discards the causally later x=2
Node 2 detects the inversion and raises an error to the client
Node 2 keeps both of the values as siblings for later merging
Node 2 discards the write x = 1 as a duplicate of the other

questions.explanation: Last-write-wins orders values by local wall-clock timestamps rather than causality. Even a few milliseconds of skew can discard a sequential update; moving timestamp generation to clients does not remove that clock error.

questions.question: What is wrong with last-write-wins? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A lagging clock can make many valid writes silently disappear
Timestamps cannot distinguish causal order from concurrency
Equal timestamps need an arbitrary tiebreaker that may violate causality
Last-write-wins causes corruption of the data as it sits on disk

questions.explanation: Three problems: vanishing writes, conflated sequential and concurrent writes, and timestamp collisions.

optionExplanations.a: A slow clock can timestamp a long sequence below an earlier fast-clock value, causing LWW to discard every one without reporting failure.
optionExplanations.b: Physical timestamps alone do not record whether one operation observed another, so LWW can order a causal update as if it were an independent concurrent write.
optionExplanations.c: Finite clock resolution lets separate nodes produce identical timestamps; an arbitrary secondary ordering resolves the tie but does not preserve causality.
optionExplanations.d: LWW discards logically valid versions according to metadata, but it does not imply byte-level corruption of the values stored on disk.

questions.question: Even with tightly synchronized clocks, what residual skew problem remains?

options.text: A packet appearing to arrive before it was sent
A packet arrives 100 ms after it was sent, which is expected
Two nodes report identical timestamps for different events
The clocks jump backward simultaneously

questions.explanation: The later increment depends on the earlier write, so placing it first contradicts causality. A few milliseconds of residual clock skew can produce that impossible timestamp order.

questions.question: Could NTP be made accurate enough that incorrect orderings cannot occur?

options.text: Probably not, since NTP accuracy is bounded by round-trip time
Yes, if GPS keeps every host within a known microsecond bound
Yes, if local-network NTP usually reports sub-millisecond error
Packet timestamps remove the need to compare machine clocks

questions.explanation: NTP estimates clock offset through messages whose one-way delays are unknown and variable. Better average accuracy cannot guarantee that every pair of sufficiently close events is ordered correctly.

questions.question: Define logical clocks and contrast them with physical clocks.

options.text: Incrementing counters rather than a quartz oscillator
Logical clocks measure elapsed time more precisely than physical clocks
Logical clocks are synchronized by NTP
Logical and physical clocks are the same thing

questions.explanation: Logical clocks do not estimate elapsed seconds; they encode happened-before relationships. That is enough to order causal events while leaving truly concurrent events unordered.

questions.question: What is the difference between clock resolution and accuracy?

options.text: Granularity versus closeness to true time
Resolution equals accuracy in modern systems
Accuracy is always better than resolution
Accuracy on a local network is nanoseconds

questions.explanation: More timestamp digits do not reduce oscillator drift or NTP uncertainty. Local-network synchronization may still be off by milliseconds, and public-internet time is often only accurate to tens of milliseconds with much larger spikes.

questions.question: How do you compute the clock uncertainty bound? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Use the attached GPS or atomic clock's stated error range
Combine local drift, server uncertainty and network round-trip time
It is exactly equal to the resolution the clock reports to callers
It is always zero on any clock that is synchronized using NTP

questions.explanation: Most systems don't expose this uncertainty: when you ask for the time using clock_gettime() the return value doesn't tell you the expected error of the timestamp, so you don't know if its confidence interval is five milliseconds or five years.

optionExplanations.a: Directly attached precision hardware comes with a manufacturer-specified error range that can form the base of the clock's uncertainty interval.
optionExplanations.b: A network-synchronized clock must allow for oscillator drift since synchronization, the server's uncertainty and uncertainty introduced by the request's network delay.
optionExplanations.c: Resolution says how finely values are represented, not how close they are to UTC; a nanosecond-granularity clock can still be milliseconds wrong.
optionExplanations.d: NTP estimates and reduces error but cannot eliminate variable one-way delay or oscillator drift, so synchronized clocks never have universally zero uncertainty.

questions.question: Describe Google's TrueTime API.

options.text: TrueTime in Spanner, which returns an explicit confidence interval
It returns a single exact timestamp guaranteed correct to the nanosecond
It returns a logical counter with no physical meaning
It returns the network round-trip time

questions.explanation: Representing time as an earliest/latest interval makes uncertainty explicit. Non-overlapping intervals establish an order; overlapping intervals honestly report that physical time cannot decide.

questions.question: Why are distributed transaction IDs hard to generate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Global monotonic IDs require cross-partition coordination
IDs must order a reader after the transaction it observed
A central ID generator becomes a high-rate bottleneck
Because a transaction ID is required to be a globally unique string value

questions.explanation: Scalable generators such as Snowflake allocate portions of an ID space across nodes and produce roughly increasing unique IDs. They avoid a central bottleneck but generally cannot guarantee increasing IDs for every causal dependency.

optionExplanations.a: One strictly increasing sequence across partitions needs nodes to coordinate ownership of the next number, adding latency and a shared serialization point.
optionExplanations.b: Snapshot visibility needs a reader transaction's ID to follow the transaction whose write it observed; uniqueness alone does not encode that causal relationship.
optionExplanations.c: Routing every small transaction through one sequence service can exhaust its throughput and make it a system-wide availability dependency.
optionExplanations.d: Transaction IDs need suitable uniqueness and ordering semantics, but they are not required to be string values; numeric and structured identifiers are common.

questions.question: State the observation Spanner's snapshot isolation is based on.

options.text: If the intervals do not overlap, the order is definitely known
If the midpoints of the intervals differ, the order is determined
If the intervals overlap, the order is determined by node ID
Interval comparison never determines order

questions.explanation: If one uncertainty interval ends before another begins, the first event definitely happened earlier. When intervals overlap, physical clocks cannot prove an order and the algorithm must preserve that uncertainty.

questions.question: Why does Spanner wait out the TrueTime uncertainty interval before commit?

options.text: To ensure later transactions receive non-overlapping time ranges
It commits immediately and resolves conflicts later; no special hardware is needed
It waits one second per transaction, using NTP only
It uses logical clocks and no waiting

questions.explanation: Waiting until the uncertainty window has passed ensures a later transaction receives a non-overlapping time interval. A 7 ms wait would limit one strictly sequential committer to roughly 143 commits per second, so parallelism and tightly synchronized hardware matter.

questions.question: How does a time-limited lease support leader failover?

options.text: The leader renews it; another node may take over after expiry
The node asks all other nodes on every write; a lease caches the answer
The node checks its own clock; a lease adds a timestamp
Leadership is permanent once granted, so the question never arises

questions.explanation: A lease grants leadership only until an expiry time. A healthy leader renews before expiry; afterward another node may acquire the role, subject to fencing stale holders.

questions.question: Why is checking a lease immediately before handling a request unsafe?

options.text: The process may pause after the check until the lease expires
It renews far too often, which wastes network bandwidth
It uses a monotonic clock, which cannot measure an expiry time
The approach is sound, provided NTP is running on every machine

questions.explanation: Clock skew can make the remaining-time calculation wrong. More fundamentally, a GC or scheduling pause can occur between validation and use; when the thread resumes, a replacement leader may already hold the lease.

questions.question: Can a concurrent garbage collector eliminate stop-the-world pauses?

options.text: No; it reduces them but some global pauses remain
GC pauses last at most a few milliseconds; concurrent collectors never stop the world
GC pauses last seconds and can be eliminated by tuning
GC pauses do not affect distributed systems

questions.explanation: During a full pause, the process cannot renew leases or respond, while other machines continue and may replace it. Concurrent collectors still require brief global pauses and cannot provide a hard maximum.

questions.question: Which causes suspend an entire machine, not just one thread? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Suspending and later resuming an entire virtual machine
Live-migrating a virtual machine between physical hosts
Suspending a laptop when its user closes the lid
Network interface resets, which suspend the CPU for their duration

questions.explanation: VM suspension, live migration and laptop sleep pause every process on the machine. The software cannot renew leases or observe elapsed work while stopped, so peers may legitimately move on.

optionExplanations.a: Suspending a virtual machine freezes all of its processes and memory image until resume, so every application thread stops together.
optionExplanations.b: Live migration may briefly stop the entire guest while final memory changes transfer and execution switches to the destination host.
optionExplanations.c: Laptop sleep halts the operating system and all processes until the user resumes the device, potentially after an arbitrary wall-clock interval.
optionExplanations.d: A network-interface reset interrupts communication but does not normally suspend the machine's CPU or every process for the reset duration.

questions.question: What is steal time in a virtualized environment?

options.text: CPU time when the host runs other VMs instead
Steal time is CPU time consumed by the garbage collector
Steal time is the time lost to clock drift between nodes
A context switch cannot pause a thread partway through a function

questions.explanation: Under load, a runnable thread may remain in a run queue for an unpredictable time. Inside a VM, the guest cannot directly see the host scheduling another tenant, so the missing CPU interval appears as steal time.

questions.question: How can unexpected synchronous disk I/O pause application code?

options.text: The thread blocks, possibly behind network storage or GC
Disk I/O only pauses threads that explicitly open files
Disk I/O pauses are bounded by the disk's seek time
Network storage eliminates I/O pauses

questions.explanation: Lazy classloading is the surprising trigger; network storage and GC are the compounding factors.

questions.question: What is memory thrashing?

options.text: Swapping dominates useful work
Thrashing means excessive garbage collection
Thrashing means excessive context switching
Paging never causes pauses on modern systems

questions.explanation: Disk-backed page recovery is far slower than memory access and can trigger another eviction. Sustained pressure creates a feedback loop of page-ins and page-outs, leaving little CPU time for useful work.

questions.question: Which signal pauses a running thread mid-execution without the thread noticing, and how is it usually sent?

options.text: The SIGSTOP signal, as sent by Ctrl-Z in a shell
SIGSTOP terminates the process permanently
SIGSTOP is only available in virtualized environments
SIGSTOP pauses only I/O, not CPU

questions.explanation: A process resumes after preemption, paging or suspension as if execution simply continued. Meanwhile deadlines, leases and other nodes' state may have advanced, making its assumptions stale.

questions.question: Why can't distributed nodes rely on ordinary shared-memory mutexes?

options.text: Nodes share no memory and communicate through unreliable messages
They transfer directly, since a distributed lock is just a mutex
They fail only because of clock skew between the machines
They fail only because of latency added by the network

questions.explanation: No shared memory is the structural reason; unnoticed pauses are the practical one.

questions.question: What defines a hard real-time system?

options.text: It meets specified deadlines in every supported circumstance
Real-time means high performance, and the two usages agree
Real-time means low latency, with no guarantee attached
The two usages are identical in meaning and in practice

questions.explanation: Hard real-time means every supported execution meets a documented deadline. Web 'real-time' usually means low-latency streaming or push under normal conditions, without a worst-case guarantee.

questions.question: What does providing real-time guarantees require, and what does it cost? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A real-time stack with bounded operations and extensive measurement
Restricted language, library and tool choices
High development cost and possibly lower throughput
For server-side data processing real-time guarantees are both economical and by now standard industry practice

questions.explanation: Hard deadlines require a real-time operating system, bounded library operations, controlled allocation and extensive worst-case testing. Those restrictions are expensive and may reduce throughput, so ordinary server systems accept pauses.

optionExplanations.a: Every software layer must document and honor worst-case timing, and measurement must verify the complete system rather than only average performance.
optionExplanations.b: Most languages and libraries permit unbounded pauses from allocation, garbage collection or blocking calls, so hard deadlines sharply narrow the usable ecosystem.
optionExplanations.c: Worst-case engineering, certification and reserved resources are expensive, and prioritizing deadlines may deliberately sacrifice aggregate throughput.
optionExplanations.d: General server-side processing normally favors utilization and flexible tooling; full hard real-time guarantees are too costly to be standard or universally economical.

questions.question: How can a service reduce the user-visible impact of garbage collection pauses?

options.text: Drain traffic or proactively restart one process at a time
Disable garbage collection entirely on the server nodes
Run a real-time operating system for all server workloads
Increase the heap size until garbage collection never runs

questions.explanation: Allocation rate and free-memory trends can warn that collection is approaching. The service can drain a node before GC or roll processes before expensive old-generation collection, hiding many pauses from clients while retaining redundancy.

questions.question: Why can one distributed node not know another node's exact state?

options.text: Silence cannot distinguish death, delay, partition or pause
Nodes share memory but not clocks, so only timing is uncertain
Nodes can determine each other's state by direct inspection
Only partial failure distinguishes distributed systems

questions.explanation: A node observes other machines only through delayed or missing messages and fallible clocks. It cannot distinguish a crash from a long pause or partition with certainty, so protocols must base decisions on evidence from multiple nodes and preserve causality despite incomplete knowledge.
