questions.question: How do you reason about an unreliable system without having to resolve every philosophical question?

options.text: State the assumptions as a system model and design to meet them
By assuming the network is reliable and testing very thoroughly
By restricting yourself to single-node systems throughout
By accepting that reliable behaviour is simply unachievable

questions.explanation: A system model states the delays and fault behaviors an algorithm may encounter. Designers can then prove safety and liveness within those assumptions and test whether the deployment plausibly satisfies them.

questions.question: Which one-sided network fault lets a node still believe it is healthy while the rest of the cluster declares it dead?

options.text: A node that receives every message but whose outgoing messages are dropped
A node whose incoming messages are dropped while its replies get through
A node whose clock is set far in the past, so its messages look stale
A node that lies in its heartbeat replies about its own health

questions.explanation: The moral: a node cannot necessarily trust its own judgment of a situation, so a distributed system cannot exclusively rely on a single node — otherwise, if that node fails, the system would be stuck and unable to recover.

questions.question: Which situations require that there be only one of some thing? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Only one node is allowed to be the leader for a database partition, to avoid split brain
Only one transaction or client is allowed to hold the lock for a particular resource or object, to prevent concurrently writing to it and corrupting it
Only one user is allowed to register a particular username, because a username must uniquely identify a user
Only one node in the whole cluster is permitted to hold a clock reading

questions.explanation: The trap: even if a node believes that it is 'the chosen one', that doesn't necessarily mean a quorum of nodes agrees. A node may have formerly been the leader, but if the other nodes declared it dead in the meantime due to a network interruption or GC pause, it may have been demoted and another leader may already have been elected — yet if it keeps acting as the chosen one and other nodes believe it, the system as a whole may do something incorrect.

optionExplanations.a: Two simultaneous partition leaders can accept incompatible writes, so election and fencing must ensure that only the current leader's actions take effect.
optionExplanations.b: Mutual exclusion protects a resource by permitting only one valid lock holder at a time, while fencing handles a holder that resumes after losing the lock.
optionExplanations.c: A username is an application uniqueness invariant: accepting two owners for the same identifier would make authentication and references ambiguous.
optionExplanations.d: Every node necessarily has a local clock reading, and distributed algorithms do not require one globally exclusive clock holder; they manage clock uncertainty instead.

questions.question: How can a paused lease holder corrupt a resource after its lease expires?

options.text: It resumes and writes after a newer lease holder
Two nodes both claim leadership and diverge; Cassandra had this bug
A clock jumps backward and writes are reordered; Riak had this bug
A network partition splits the cluster; ZooKeeper had this bug

questions.explanation: A lease prevents overlap only while every writer respects its current validity. A paused process cannot notice expiry; after a replacement writer starts, the stale holder can resume and issue a conflicting write unless the storage service fences it.

questions.question: How does a fencing token stop a stale lease holder?

options.text: The resource rejects tokens older than the greatest seen
A fencing token is a timestamp; the server rejects older timestamps
A fencing token is a client ID; the server accepts only the newest client
A fencing token is a checksum of the write

questions.explanation: The resource remembers the greatest token it has processed. A client may incorrectly believe an expired lease remains valid, but it cannot make progress because its older token proves that a newer owner has already acted.

questions.question: Which ZooKeeper values can act as monotonically increasing fencing tokens?

options.text: zxid transaction IDs or cversion node versions
The session ID and the ephemeral node path; the client must check
The server timestamp and the watch counter; the lock service must check
ZooKeeper does not provide suitable tokens

questions.explanation: Client-side lease checks are insufficient because a client can pause between checking and writing. Only the storage service sees the final operation and can compare its token with newer accepted operations.

questions.question: A resource rejects any writer presenting a stale fencing token. Which class of node misbehavior does that protect against?

options.text: A node acting in error, such as one whose lease has quietly expired
Fencing tokens defend against all faults, including malice
Fencing tokens defend only against clock skew between nodes
A node forging a higher token number to push out the holder

questions.explanation: Fencing blocks an honest but stale process that has not learned its lease expired. It does not defend against a malicious client that forges a higher token; that stronger arbitrary behavior belongs to the Byzantine fault model.

questions.question: Describe the Two Generals Problem.

options.text: Two generals who must agree but can only send unreliable messengers
Two generals must agree even though one of them is a traitor
Two generals share a radio channel that may be jammed
Two generals must synchronize their clocks before attacking

questions.explanation: Lost and delayed messengers, with no traitors — that is the non-Byzantine version.

questions.question: How does the Byzantine version differ?

options.text: n generals who must agree while some among them are traitors
There are exactly three generals, one of whom is known to be a traitor
All generals are traitors
The messengers are traitors rather than the generals

questions.explanation: Byzantine agreement must reach a consistent decision even when some participants send contradictory or deceptive messages. Honest nodes do not initially know which participants are faulty.

questions.question: What does the term Byzantine fault refer to?

options.text: Arbitrary, inconsistent or deceptive component behavior
It refers to documented treachery among Byzantine generals
It refers to the Byzantine Empire's cryptographic systems
It was coined by Kyle Kingsbury

questions.explanation: Lamport chose a deliberately non-current nationality, but the technical name relies on the established figurative meaning of 'Byzantine.' Historical Byzantium is background, not the etymological reason for the fault model.

questions.question: Define Byzantine fault-tolerant.

options.text: It keeps operating correctly even when nodes disobey the protocol
If it tolerates only malicious attackers, not malfunctioning nodes
If it tolerates only malfunctioning nodes, not attackers
If it tolerates network partitions

questions.explanation: Note both halves: the nodes need not be adversarial to be Byzantine — merely arbitrary.

questions.question: Why must flight control systems tolerate Byzantine faults?

options.text: Radiation corrupting memory or registers in aerospace systems
Because a pilot may deliberately issue a malicious command
Because flight software is written by untrusted outside vendors
Because air traffic control networks are publicly accessible

questions.explanation: Cosmic rays, faulty memory, disk corruption and network errors can produce arbitrary-looking values without an attacker. Byzantine behavior describes the observed failure, not necessarily malicious intent.

questions.question: What is the second circumstance where Byzantine fault tolerance is relevant?

options.text: Multiple organizations, where some participants may try to defraud others
In single-organization datacenters, where insiders may be malicious
In web applications, where browsers are untrusted
In embedded systems, where hardware may be counterfeit

questions.explanation: Absence of a central authority among mutually untrusting parties is the defining condition.

questions.question: Why do most server-side data systems assume no Byzantine faults? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Nodes are usually inside one organizational trust boundary, and radiation-induced memory corruption is rare enough not to dominate the fault model
Datacenter hardware makes arbitrary corruption physically impossible
Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols are substantially more complicated and may require hardware support
The deployment and replication cost is impractical for most server-side systems

questions.explanation: The assumption is pragmatic, not absolute: controlled nodes are usually honest, arbitrary hardware corruption is uncommon, and full Byzantine protocols add substantial complexity and replica cost. Security controls still remain necessary.

optionExplanations.a: Servers under one operator are normally authenticated and administered together, while random arbitrary memory corruption is rare enough that crash faults dominate routine design.
optionExplanations.b: Datacenter hardware can suffer memory, CPU, disk and network corruption; non-Byzantine models are an economic assumption, not a claim of physical impossibility.
optionExplanations.c: Byzantine agreement needs more complex protocols and sometimes trusted hardware or cryptography to handle participants that send inconsistent messages.
optionExplanations.d: Tolerating Byzantine faults usually needs substantially more replicas and communication, making the deployment cost unattractive for ordinary server applications.

questions.question: How do web applications normally handle arbitrary behavior from end-user clients?

options.text: Validate and authorize at a trusted server
Other servers in the same datacenter; they use Byzantine consensus
Database replicas; they use quorum voting
Network switches; they use checksums

questions.explanation: Browsers and other user-controlled clients cannot be trusted to follow protocol. A web service normally relies on its own trusted servers to authenticate identities, authorize actions and validate every submitted value.

questions.question: Why can't a Byzantine fault-tolerant algorithm save you from your own bugs?

options.text: Because the same buggy software on every node defeats the algorithm
Because a software bug is not a Byzantine fault by definition
Because Byzantine algorithms require unanimity among nodes
It can save you, provided that the bug is sufficiently rare

questions.explanation: With n = 4, more than two-thirds means more than 2.67 nodes correct, so at least 3 correct and therefore at most 1 faulty — and the same bug in the same code breaks all four.

questions.question: Could a protocol protect against vulnerabilities and compromise?

options.text: Because an attacker who compromises one node can likely compromise all
Yes — Byzantine fault tolerance solves the security problem completely
Yes, provided that fewer than one-third of the nodes are compromised
No, and there is no protection of any kind against this

questions.explanation: Homogeneity of software defeats the quorum assumption for attackers as well as for bugs.

questions.question: What can basic validation and checksums defend against?

options.text: Corruption, bugs and misconfiguration, not determined attackers
They constitute full Byzantine fault tolerance at a low cost
They defend successfully against a determined adversary
Such guards are not worth implementing in any server-side system

questions.explanation: These checks cheaply reject accidental nonsense and isolated misconfiguration. An attacker can deliberately forge internally consistent values, so full Byzantine tolerance would require stronger identities, quorums, and independent implementations.

questions.question: Why add an application-level checksum above TCP or UDP?

options.text: Transport checksums do not catch every end-to-end corruption
TCP checksums are sufficient; no application-level check is needed
Full cryptographic signing is required on every packet
Packet corruption does not occur in modern networks

questions.explanation: Transport checksums protect individual packets imperfectly and may not cover corruption elsewhere in the path. An end-to-end application checksum validates the actual message received.

questions.question: What validation should internal services perform on received messages?

options.text: Basic protocol, range, size and sanity checks
Public applications need no checks; internal ones need strict checks
Both need identical, maximally strict checks
Checks are unnecessary on either side, provided the connection uses TLS

questions.explanation: A firewall changes the likelihood of hostile input, not the possibility of corrupted, buggy, or misconfigured messages. Validation can be proportionate to the trust boundary but should never disappear entirely.

questions.question: How does an NTP client identify a misconfigured server?

options.text: Compare several uncertainty ranges and discard an outlier
The client uses only the first responding server
The client averages all servers including outliers
The client trusts the server with the lowest stratum number unconditionally

questions.explanation: No single external time server is fully trustworthy. Agreement among independent estimates makes one server that is hours wrong detectable, provided most configured sources are reasonably correct.

questions.question: What is a distributed-system model?

options.text: An abstraction of the delays and faults an algorithm assumes
A system model is a benchmark of the system's performance
A system model is a diagram of the deployment topology
A system model is the concrete implementation of an algorithm

questions.explanation: A proof is meaningful only relative to assumptions about delays, pauses, crashes, recovery, and arbitrary behavior. A system model states those assumptions explicitly so an algorithm can be evaluated independently of one deployment.

questions.question: What bounds does the synchronous system model assume?

options.text: Finite bounds on network delay, process pauses and clock error
It assumes zero delay and perfectly synchronized clocks, and is realistic
It assumes unbounded delay, and is the realistic choice
It assumes there are no clocks in the system at all

questions.explanation: An algorithm may tolerate nonzero latency and clock skew if a known maximum exists. Commodity networks and runtimes occasionally exceed any chosen bound, so the model is useful for reasoning but not a faithful worst-case description.

questions.question: What does the partially synchronous model assume?

options.text: Useful bounds usually, but unbounded delays during some faults
It means the delays are always large, but nonetheless bounded
It means clocks are synchronized even though networks are not
The model does not describe any system that has actually been deployed

questions.explanation: The model captures both operational experience: healthy systems are usually timely enough to make progress, yet overload, partitions, and pauses can violate every normal timeout. Algorithms must preserve safety during those unbounded intervals.

questions.question: What is an algorithm forbidden from doing in the asynchronous model?

options.text: No timing assumptions at all, and not even a clock
It cannot send messages at all, only receive them
It cannot make use of any persistent storage
It cannot assume that the other nodes are honest

questions.explanation: A fully asynchronous model assumes no clocks and no upper bound on message delay or process pauses. Timeout-based failure detection is therefore unavailable, making liveness much harder to guarantee.

questions.question: Match the timing models to their defining statements.

options.text: Synchronous has fixed bounds; partially synchronous exceeds them sometimes
Synchronous has no clock; asynchronous has bounded delay
Partially synchronous has no clock; synchronous is occasionally unbounded
All three assume bounded delay, differing only in clock accuracy

questions.explanation: Hard synchronous timing bounds are unrealistic for ordinary services. Partial synchrony models normal bounded behavior plus rare disruption; a fully asynchronous model assumes no timing information and is very restrictive.

questions.question: State the crash-stop assumption, including what makes it stop rather than merely crash.

options.text: That a node fails only by crashing and never comes back
The node crashes and recovers after a known delay
The node crashes and recovers with its memory intact
The node slows down but never stops

questions.explanation: Crash-stop assumes a failed node never participates again. Crash-recovery allows it to restart, so algorithms must reason about surviving state and how the returning node catches up.

questions.question: Give the crash-recovery assumptions, being precise about state.

options.text: Nodes may crash and later recover, with stable storage surviving
In-memory state survives a crash while disk state is lost
Both in-memory and on-disk state survive a node crash
Both kinds of state are lost, but the recovery time is known in advance

questions.explanation: With stable storage, volatile memory is lost in a crash but persisted state survives. The model does not promise when recovery occurs, so peers cannot wait for a known restart deadline.

questions.question: State the Byzantine node model, and why does 'arbitrary' matter?

options.text: Nodes may do absolutely anything, including deceiving other nodes
Nodes are always adversarial, being controlled by an attacker
Nodes may only crash or slow down, never behave arbitrarily
Nodes may lie, but only about timing and never about data

questions.explanation: Byzantine faults allow any protocol deviation: lies, contradictions, corrupted messages or nonsensical state. The model covers malicious behavior and severe accidental corruption alike.

questions.question: Of the nine combinations of timing and node models, which is the most useful?

options.text: Partially synchronous with crash-recovery faults
The synchronous model with crash-stop faults
The asynchronous model with Byzantine faults
The synchronous model with Byzantine faults

questions.explanation: Partially synchronous timing matches systems that are usually responsive but sometimes suffer unbounded pauses. Crash-recovery with stable storage matches nodes that restart after losing memory while retaining durable state.
